S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, including incidents initially reported by customers or third parties. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk for their model, and provide material updates promptly.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, including incidents initially reported by customers or third parties. A preliminary report may be updated as facts are confirmed. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk for their model, and provide material updates promptly. Annual reports must include incident counts and installed-unit denominators by model, submitted to regulators.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and after material design changes, using a statistically representative sample and a documented protocol. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notice to the regulator, a corrective-action plan, and retesting within a regulator-approved period.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and after material design changes, using a statistically representative sample and a documented protocol. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notice to the regulator, a corrective-action plan, and retesting within a regulator-approved period. Regulators may restrict or suspend sale where the evidence indicates an imminent or serious safety risk, or where corrective action is not completed on time. Manufacturers must submit complete per-model results to the regulator and provide those results, including the model’s failure rate, to customers who buy that model. Individual-company per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public. Regulators may impose proportionate additional measures based on the model’s risk and corrective-action progress.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off, with appropriate safeguards against unauthorized activation. For already-installed units that do not support the function, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent upgrade within six years of this standard taking effect.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off, with appropriate safeguards against unauthorized activation. For already-installed units that do not support the function, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent upgrade within six years of this standard taking effect.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off, with appropriate safeguards against unauthorized activation. For already-installed units that do not support the function, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent upgrade within six years of this standard taking effect. Where a safe retrofit is not technically feasible, the manufacturer must notify affected customers and the regulator and provide an approved alternative safety measure.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must document that the system is suitable for the battery’s hazards and provide installation, maintenance, and customer safety instructions.

parameters.quote: If a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, calculated using all known and substantiated incidents and the installed-unit denominator, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan. Regulators must promptly assess the model and determine proportionate measures, which may include a recall, based on the evidence and the effectiveness of corrective action.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: If a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, calculated using all known and substantiated incidents and the installed-unit denominator, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan. Regulators must promptly assess the model and determine proportionate measures, which may include a recall, based on the evidence and the effectiveness of corrective action.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive model-specific safety information, including known material hazards, emergency instructions, material safety findings, and complete per-model 55 °C test results, including the failure rate. Manufacturers must submit complete per-model test results and annual thermal-incident rates, with installed-unit denominators, to regulators and promptly notify affected customers of material safety findings, providing updates as information changes. Individual-company per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public. If a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, calculated using all known and substantiated incidents and the installed-unit denominator, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan. Regulators must promptly assess the model and determine proportionate measures, which may include a recall, based on the evidence and the effectiveness of corrective action. Regulators may require corrective action or a recall below the threshold when evidence indicates an imminent or serious safety risk.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: Halcyon’s figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units last year; the Ember 8 flagship was 9.9 per 100,000. Four thermal incidents last year were not reported to any regulator. The flagship’s 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate was 3.9%. Remote emergency shut-off is supported by 81% of installed units. Built-in fire suppression would cost about $67 per unit. These data support reporting all thermal incidents and transparent per-model test results, including to customers.

The Hearth 10 rate was 6.4 per 100,000; its 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate was 6.2%. judge_section_notes: The final rules keep S1 strict on reporting and customer notice. S2 sets a 55 °C test and a 5% failure benchmark but allows continued sale with corrective action and regulator discretion, while giving per-model failure rates to customers but not the public. S3 requires new-unit shut-off immediately and retrofit within six years; S4 requires built-in suppression from 36 months; S5 sets an 8/100k threshold for notification and corrective-action plans but leaves recall to regulator discretion.
